paragraphs: This paper challenges the widespread recommendation to prefer AUPRC over AUROC whenever a classification dataset has imbalanced classes. The authors analyze how both metrics respond to model mistakes. Their conclusion is that class imbalance alone does not establish AUPRC as the better tool for comparing models; the behavior of the metric needs closer examination.

The analysis also identifies a fairness concern. AUPRC can give disproportionate credit to improvements within subpopulations where positive labels are more common. Consequently, a model comparison based on that metric can favor changes that increase disparities. Experiments using both semi-synthetic data and real-world fairness datasets support the theoretical account of this possible problem.

The authors then review more than 1.5 million scientific papers to investigate how the recommendation spread. They find unsupported assertions, citations that do not support the claim, and conclusions extended beyond their original scope. The combined contribution is a more precise account of these metrics and evidence that a familiar evaluation rule can become misleading when treated as universally applicable.
neurips-2024-a-closer-look-at-auroc-and-.tldr: Class imbalance does not generally make AUPRC superior to AUROC, and favoring it can sometimes worsen subgroup disparities.

paragraphs: The paper asks how much information about a scene’s physical structure is present inside large vision models. Its lightweight testing protocol takes features from an existing model and trains classifiers to predict annotated physical properties in real images. This makes physical understanding measurable through the information that those classifiers can extract from the features.

The authors apply the protocol to geometry, materials, support relations, lighting, and properties that depend on viewpoint. They compare CLIP, DINOv1, DINOv2, VQGAN, and Stable Diffusion. Stable Diffusion and DINOv2 provide useful features for learning several properties, including depth, shadows, and support relations. Their performance is weaker on occlusion and materials, although they outperform the other tested models across the properties examined.

A further finding is that the choice of internal features matters: different network layers and different Stable Diffusion time steps work well for different properties. The results therefore provide guidance about where useful physical information can be found. The evidence concerns information recoverable by trained probes, giving a concrete interpretation to the paper’s question about physical understanding.
neurips-2024-a-general-protocol-to-probe.tldr: A lightweight probing protocol finds useful but uneven information about 3D physical properties in large vision models.

paragraphs: Models trained on biased datasets can rely on spurious correlations that do not support reliable generalization. One approach to correcting this behavior is to find examples that contradict those correlations and use them to improve training. The difficulty is identifying these valuable examples accurately, especially in the setting motivating this work, where bias knowledge or an unbiased reference set is unavailable.

The paper approaches that detection problem through a connection to mislabeled examples. It draws on similarities between samples that conflict with a dataset’s bias and samples studied in label-error detection. Specifically, the authors investigate influence functions as a way to identify bias-conflicting samples, then use those samples to remedy the biased model.

Analysis and experiments across diverse datasets show improved detection precision and effective correction of biased models. The method also improves models that have already received recent debiasing treatments. This complementarity matters because better sample identification can contribute additional gains even after another technique has addressed bias, rather than requiring the entire training approach to be replaced.
neurips-2024-a-simple-remedy-for-dataset.tldr: Using influence functions to detect bias-conflicting samples improves debiasing and can complement existing correction methods.

paragraphs: AliDiff addresses how to steer molecule generators toward properties desirable for a particular protein target. Existing target-aware diffusion models learn distributions of candidate molecules, but that alone provides limited control over the quality of their outputs. The paper introduces an alignment framework that starts with a pretrained model and changes which molecules it tends to generate.

The framework uses preference optimization with user-defined rewards to favor higher binding affinity and more reasonable molecular structures. To address overfitting associated with common preference objectives, the authors develop Exact Energy Preference Optimization. They also give a closed-form description of the distribution reached at convergence, making the intended result of alignment mathematically explicit.

Experiments on CrossDocked2020 report state-of-the-art binding energies, including an average Vina score reaching -7.07, while retaining strong molecular properties. The stated result concerns generated molecules and their benchmark evaluations. The broader contribution is a general way to connect target-conditioned generation with explicit functional preferences, so that learning the candidate distribution and steering its outputs become parts of the same workflow.
neurips-2024-aligning-target-aware-molec.tldr: AliDiff aligns pretrained molecule diffusion models with user-defined rewards to improve binding energies while preserving strong molecular properties.

paragraphs: Cancer detection models can struggle when tissue images come from a different hospital. Fixation, staining, and imaging equipment all affect appearance, creating differences between training images and later inputs. This paper investigates whether emphasizing cell nuclei can improve transfer across those differences, motivated by the importance of nuclear shape and organization for detecting cancer.

The proposed training approach combines original tissue images with segmentation masks that identify nuclei. These masks direct attention toward nuclear morphology and spatial arrangement, which the authors treat as domain-invariant features. The method also aligns the internal representations of original images and masks through regularization. That additional constraint makes the masks a direct influence on what the model learns to represent.

Across multiple datasets, the authors report better generalization outside the training domain, together with greater robustness to image corruptions and adversarial attacks. These findings support the proposed emphasis on nuclei in the evaluated cancer-detection setting. The contribution is a simple training strategy that connects a biologically relevant image structure with a representation constraint intended to reduce sensitivity to hospital-specific appearance.
neurips-2024-are-nuclear-masks-all-you-n.tldr: Training with nuclear masks and aligned image representations improves cancer-detection generalization across datasets and increases robustness.

paragraphs: The paper studies whether a causal effect within a particular subpopulation can be computed from observational data collected in that same subpopulation. This is the subpopulation identification problem, or s-ID. Earlier work addressed the setting where every variable in the system is observable. The authors extend the problem to allow latent variables, meaning variables that are not observed.

Their approach begins by adapting graphical concepts used in the classical causal identification problem. In particular, they develop counterparts of c-components and Hedges for the subpopulation setting with latent variables. These definitions provide the structural language needed to reason about identification when both the restriction to a subpopulation and unobserved variables are present.

Using this extended framework, the authors propose a sound identification algorithm. Soundness means that the causal identification conclusions the algorithm produces are valid within the framework. The stated contribution therefore expands the setting in which correct identification can be established. The abstract claims soundness, so its result should be understood as a correctness guarantee for the algorithm’s conclusions, without assuming a stronger claim that it resolves every identifiable case.
neurips-2024-causal-effect-identificatio.tldr: The paper extends subpopulation causal identification to latent-variable settings and provides a sound algorithm.

paragraphs: ChaosBench evaluates climate prediction over subseasonal-to-seasonal horizons, where extending an ordinary weather forecast becomes difficult. At these timescales, interactions between parts of the Earth system and the growth of small errors matter alongside initial conditions. The benchmark addresses shortcomings in existing evaluations that typically cover shorter horizons, limited operational comparisons, and insufficient checks of physical consistency.

Its data combine atmospheric information with ocean, ice, and land reanalysis products spanning more than 45 years. Evaluation includes deterministic, probabilistic, and physics-based metrics, with attention to ensembles and boundary conditions. The authors compare data-driven weather models with physics-based forecasts from four national weather agencies, creating a broader basis for assessing performance.

The evaluated methods originally developed for weather timescales lose predictive skill on the longer task, falling back to performance characterized as unskilled climatology. The paper also demonstrates strategies that can extend their useful forecasting range: ensembles, better control of error propagation, and physics-informed models. Together, these results make ChaosBench both a demanding test of current capabilities and a way to evaluate concrete approaches to longer-range prediction.
neurips-2024-chaosbench-a-multi-channel-.tldr: ChaosBench exposes weaknesses in longer-range climate forecasting and evaluates strategies for extending weather models’ predictive skill.

paragraphs: DiffPO tackles the problem of predicting outcomes under interventions using observational data. The paper is motivated by medical decision-making, where a single predicted outcome can leave out important information about uncertainty. Its objective is to learn distributions of potential outcomes, giving a richer description of what an intervention could produce than a point estimate alone.

The method uses a conditional denoising diffusion model tailored to this causal task. This component learns complex outcome distributions, while a specially designed orthogonal diffusion loss addresses selection bias. The two pieces connect flexible distribution modeling with the need to account for how observational data were selected, which is central to the paper’s approach.

The authors also describe DiffPO as flexible enough to estimate other causal quantities, including conditional average treatment effects. Experiments across a wide range of settings report state-of-the-art performance. The stated contribution is therefore both a distribution-learning method and a reusable basis for different causal estimates, with the distributional focus intended to retain information about potential outcomes that conventional point predictions typically discard.
neurips-2024-diffpo-a-causal-diffusion-m.tldr: DiffPO combines conditional diffusion with a selection-bias-aware loss to learn distributions of potential intervention outcomes.

paragraphs: This paper builds a benchmark for comparing how humans and vision models infer object identity across changes in viewpoint. Given several images, participants decide whether they show the same object or different objects. The images include familiar categories such as chairs and procedurally generated abstract shapes, so the task covers more than recognition of familiar objects.

The researchers construct over 2,000 image sets and collect 35,000 behavioral trials from more than 500 people. They record choices along with reaction times and gaze information. These additional measurements help characterize how people handle the task, extending the comparison beyond a single accuracy score. Models evaluated include DINOv2, MAE, and CLIP.

Humans outperform every tested model by a wide margin. At the same time, human and model performance are correlated, indicating some shared pattern in which cases are difficult. The analysis also finds that humans devote more time or processing to challenging trials. The benchmark thus reveals both overlap in task difficulty and a substantial gap in successful recognition across viewpoints, while providing behavioral data for studying that gap.
neurips-2024-evaluating-multiview-object.tldr: Humans substantially outperform tested vision models at recognizing objects across viewpoints, despite correlated patterns of difficulty.

paragraphs: This paper considers federated learning where clients have unlabeled data and only the server has a small labeled collection. Such a setup can perform substantially worse than centralized semi-supervised learning. The authors attribute the gap to confirmation bias: training reinforces incorrect model-generated labels, with repeated local training and the separation of labeled and unlabeled data making the problem more pronounced.

Their method, (FL)², introduces sharpness-aware consistency regularization for client training. The authors find that applying regularization to the original pseudo-labeling loss is suboptimal, so they carefully select which unlabeled samples receive it. This selection makes the regularization strategy a targeted part of learning from uncertain labels.

The framework also adapts thresholds separately for each client and adjusts aggregation according to clients’ learning progress. These mechanisms let training respond to differences in how clients are learning. On three benchmark datasets, the method substantially improves performance and bridges the gap with centralized semi-supervised learning, particularly when labeled examples are scarce. The result supports coordinating sample selection, local adaptation, and aggregation when supervision is concentrated at the server.
neurips-2024-fl-2-overcoming-few-labels-.tldr: (FL)² improves federated learning with unlabeled clients through selective regularization and training adjustments based on client progress.

paragraphs: The paper addresses the difficulty of controlling individual objects in text-to-image generation. High-quality output can require extensive prompt adjustment, and layout conditioning still leaves limits on editing and detailed object attributes. The proposed approach divides generation into stages so that object appearance can be established before those objects are assembled into a complete scene.

A new training procedure adapts a diffusion model to produce isolated scene components as RGBA images, which include transparency information. These separately generated instances then become inputs to a multilayer composition process. The composition stage smoothly assembles them into realistic images, supporting control over both the components themselves and how they are placed together.

Experiments show diverse, high-quality instances with precise attribute control. The authors also demonstrate building and manipulating scenes from highly complex prompts, with detailed control over object appearance and location. They report greater control than competing methods. The significance of the staged design is that generating an object and arranging a scene become separately controllable steps, supporting the flexibility and interactivity that motivated the work.
neurips-2024-generating-compositional-sc.tldr: Generating transparent object images before multilayer composition enables finer control over scene appearance, placement, and editing.

paragraphs: Offline model-based optimization searches for good designs using a learned approximation of an objective, without querying the true objective during the search. This setting matters when actual evaluations are prohibitively expensive, as in the applications motivating the paper. A central difficulty is that the search can encounter regions where the learned surrogate makes inaccurate predictions.

The authors introduce adaptive source critic regularization, or aSCR, to constrain optimization trajectories toward regions where the surrogate is reliable. The framework is designed to work across tasks and optimizers. It includes a computationally tractable algorithm that changes the strength of the constraint dynamically, making the restriction adjustable as optimization proceeds.

The paper evaluates aSCR together with standard Bayesian optimization on a suite of offline generative design tasks and reports performance above existing methods. This finding supports the usefulness of controlling where a surrogate-guided search travels. The contribution is a general regularization framework for the search process, with an adaptive mechanism intended to keep optimization tied to the parts of the design space where its learned objective can be trusted.
neurips-2024-generative-adversarial-mode.tldr: Adaptive source critic regularization improves offline design optimization by constraining searches toward regions with reliable surrogate predictions.

paragraphs: Recovering human movement from a single video can produce jitter and poses that are physically implausible. Physics-based simulation helps, but imperfect physical models can introduce their own difficulties. Existing controller-based approaches often depend on simplifying assumptions and extensive preprocessing. This paper proposes an online method that selectively combines motion observations with simulated dynamics.

The system uses a meta-PD control loop to predict internal joint torques and external reaction forces, then performs physics-based motion simulation. A recurrent neural network implements a Kalman-filter-inspired step that attentively balances observed joint motion with the simulation. This filtering lets the estimated state reflect both sources while compensating for their respective shortcomings.

The authors find that the filtering step supplies crucial online supervision for accurate global movement trajectories and physically plausible poses. Their method performs strongly in physics-based human pose estimation and produces physically plausible predictive dynamics compared with state-of-the-art approaches. The central contribution is the learned balancing process: incorporating physics effectively depends on how simulated motion and visual observations inform one another during estimation.
neurips-2024-optimal-state-dynamics-esti.tldr: A learned filtering loop balances video-derived motion with physics simulation to improve human motion estimates and physical plausibility.

paragraphs: OTTER addresses a mismatch between the label distribution reflected in a pretrained zero-shot model and the distribution needed for a downstream task. Unbalanced web-scale pretraining data can leave models with harmful prediction tendencies. Existing correction methods may require labeled downstream examples or knowledge of pretraining label frequencies, requirements that do not fit the intended zero-shot setting.

The proposed method adjusts pretrained predictions through optimal transport. Its required task-specific input is an estimate of the downstream label distribution. This makes the correction lightweight while retaining an explicit dependency on that estimate. The theoretical analysis characterizes improvements under certain mild conditions and bounds the error introduced when the distribution estimate is misspecified.

Experiments cover zero-shot image and text classification, reporting average accuracy improvements of 4.8% and 15.9%, respectively. OTTER also beats baselines such as prior matching on 17 of 21 datasets, often by substantial margins. The results support distribution adjustment as a practical way to improve pretrained predictions, while the theory makes clear that its guarantees are conditional and account for imperfect estimates.
neurips-2024-otter-effortless-label-dist.tldr: OTTER uses optimal transport and an estimated downstream label distribution to improve zero-shot classification predictions.

paragraphs: Out-of-distribution detection identifies samples that do not fit the expected data distribution. Many unsupervised approaches use a generative model, but require a separately trained model for each inlier dataset. This paper investigates whether one existing generative model can support detection across different tasks, reducing the need to repeat model training for each new distribution.

The proposed method, Diffusion Paths or DiffPath, uses a single diffusion model originally trained for unconditional generation. It examines the paths that connect input samples to a standard normal distribution. Specifically, it measures how quickly those paths change and how they curve. These path properties become the information used for detecting unusual samples.

Across extensive experiments involving different distributions, DiffPath is competitive with previous methods that use individual models for their respective tasks. The finding supports reuse of a single diffusion model across a variety of detection problems. Its distinctive contribution is to extract detection information from the behavior of diffusion paths, showing that a model trained for generation can also supply useful signals for identifying distributional differences.
neurips-2024-out-of-distribution-detecti.tldr: DiffPath uses diffusion-path changes and curvature to perform competitive out-of-distribution detection across tasks with one generative model.

paragraphs: Language Feedback Models identify actions worth imitating when learning to follow instructions. The idea is to judge whether behavior helps complete the requested task, then use those judgments to improve imitation learning. To train these feedback models, the authors translate visual trajectories into language descriptions and obtain feedback about them from large language models.

Using the resulting models to select desirable behavior improves task completion over strong behavioral cloning baselines in Touchdown, ScienceWorld, and ALFWorld. The authors also compare this use of language models with asking them to predict actions directly. When the number of language-model output tokens is controlled, the feedback-model approach performs better.

The feedback models also transfer to unseen environments, where one round of adaptation raises task-completion rates by 3.5–12.0%. A modified version provides feedback that humans can interpret without losing performance, enabling people to verify which behaviors are being selected for imitation. These findings support learned behavioral evaluation as a useful route from language-model feedback to better instruction-following policies, including adaptation beyond the environments used initially.
neurips-2024-policy-improvement-using-la.tldr: Language Feedback Models improve instruction-following policies by identifying useful behavior to imitate and supporting adaptation to unseen environments.

paragraphs: QUEEN targets online video that viewers can inspect from different viewpoints. Streaming this kind of content requires a 3D representation that updates as frames arrive, renders quickly, and remains compact enough to transmit. The method uses 3D Gaussian Splatting and learns changes in Gaussian attributes between consecutive frames without imposing structural constraints on those changes.

Its compression strategy treats different attributes differently. A learned latent decoder quantizes changes to attributes other than position, while a learned gating module makes position changes sparse. To help distinguish moving content from static content, the system uses differences in Gaussian viewspace gradients. That signal guides sparsity learning and accelerates training.

On diverse free-viewpoint video benchmarks, QUEEN outperforms state-of-the-art online methods on all evaluated metrics. For several highly dynamic scenes, the authors report a model size of 0.7 MB per frame, training under five seconds, and rendering at approximately 350 frames per second. These results show how learning and compressing frame-to-frame changes can jointly improve reconstruction, storage, and processing efficiency in the evaluated streaming setting.
neurips-2024-queen-quantized-efficient-e.tldr: QUEEN compresses frame-to-frame Gaussian changes to deliver compact, fast, high-quality free-viewpoint video representations.

paragraphs: RAMP addresses robustness to adversarial perturbations measured by multiple norms. Training against one norm can leave a model vulnerable under others, while improving robustness can also reduce accuracy on ordinary inputs. The paper targets union accuracy, which assesses robustness across the considered perturbation types, together with maintaining useful clean accuracy.

The authors analyze these tradeoffs through distribution shifts and design a logit-pairing loss to improve union accuracy. They also use gradient projection to connect natural training with adversarial training, bringing useful information from ordinary examples into the robust training process. Both theoretical and empirical results support a moderation of the accuracy–robustness tradeoff. The framework supports full adversarial training and robust fine-tuning.

For fine-tuning, reported union accuracy reaches 53.3% on CIFAR-10 and 29.1% on ImageNet. Training ResNet-18 from scratch on CIFAR-10 yields 44.6% union accuracy against AutoAttack and 81.2% clean accuracy. The authors additionally report generalization to a range of unseen adversaries and natural corruptions. These results broaden the evaluated robustness beyond the specific perturbation types used in the main training objective.
neurips-2024-ramp-boosting-adversarial-r.tldr: RAMP combines logit pairing and gradient projection to improve robustness across multiple perturbation norms while moderating accuracy tradeoffs.

paragraphs: Designing heuristics for difficult combinatorial optimization problems often involves substantial expert trial and error. This paper introduces Language Hyper-Heuristics, which use large language models to generate heuristics with little manual intervention. Their search space is open-ended, allowing generated solutions to extend beyond a narrowly predefined collection of heuristic choices.

The proposed ReEvo method combines evolutionary search with language-model reflection. Evolution provides a way to explore candidate heuristics, while reflections offer verbal guidance about how that search might improve. The authors describe this guidance as verbal gradients: language feedback that helps direct exploration through the heuristic space.

Evaluation spans five algorithmic types and six combinatorial optimization problems, with both white-box and black-box views of the problems. ReEvo produces state-of-the-art or competitive methods across metaheuristics, evolutionary algorithms, heuristics, and neural solvers, while using samples more efficiently than earlier Language Hyper-Heuristics. The results support combining candidate search with reflective feedback as a broadly useful approach to automated algorithm design across the tested problem and algorithm families.
neurips-2024-reevo-large-language-models.tldr: ReEvo combines evolutionary search with language-model reflections to generate competitive optimization heuristics more sample-efficiently.

paragraphs: SCRREAM addresses a ground-truth problem in evaluating indoor 3D reconstruction. Large datasets often prioritize scale, but their meshes can be incomplete. When those meshes are used to produce reference depth images, missing geometry can make evaluation of fine details inaccurate. The paper therefore focuses on creating sufficiently dense and accurate annotations for geometry tasks.

The framework annotates fully dense object meshes and registers camera poses against real image sequences. This combination supports accurate reference data for both sparse and dense 3D tasks. The authors describe the annotation pipeline and illustrate four dataset variants covering indoor reconstruction and SLAM, scene editing and object removal, human reconstruction, and 6D pose estimation.

Recent indoor reconstruction and SLAM pipelines are evaluated as benchmarks. The dataset design enables dense geometry evaluation on eleven example scenes using accurately rendered reference depth maps. The central contribution is the connection between detailed scene annotation and reliable evaluation: improving the reference geometry makes it possible to assess details that incomplete indoor meshes could otherwise score incorrectly.
neurips-2024-scrream-scan-register-rende.tldr: SCRREAM combines dense mesh annotation with camera registration to provide more accurate ground truth for indoor 3D evaluation.

paragraphs: Self-supervised adversarial training aims to learn robust features without labels. The authors find that a simple benchmark still shows a large robust generalization gap and degraded performance on natural samples. They hypothesize that insufficient data complexity and model regularization contribute to these problems, motivating a method called DAQ-SDP.

The first component uses diversely augmented samples as queries that guide adversarial training. This challenges an earlier conclusion that complex augmentation harms robustness in this setting. The second component introduces a self-supervised double-perturbation scheme, inspired by work on supervised adversarial training, to encourage robustness that carries over to downstream classification.

The approach can be combined with models pretrained using different self-supervised frameworks without changing their learning objectives. Across those frameworks, it improves both robust accuracy and accuracy on natural inputs, helping narrow the gap with supervised adversarial training. The findings support the particular use of augmentation and regularization proposed here, while the authors’ explanation of the original performance problems remains explicitly a hypothesis motivating the design.
neurips-2024-self-supervised-adversarial.tldr: DAQ-SDP improves label-free adversarial training through diverse augmented queries and a self-supervised double-perturbation scheme.

paragraphs: Federated learning allows clients to collaborate on a shared model while keeping their data with them. Researchers commonly simulate this process to test ideas quickly, but simulation speed can restrict the size and realism of experiments. This paper introduces pfl-research, a Python framework intended to make those experiments faster and easier to develop.

The framework supports TensorFlow, PyTorch, and models outside neural networks. Its modular design is tightly integrated with privacy algorithms, allowing private federated learning research within the same simulation environment. This combination addresses both the computational demands of running experiments and the need to work across different modeling approaches.

In comparisons on common cross-device setups, pfl-research runs 7–72 times faster than alternative open-source frameworks. The authors argue that this speed can improve research productivity and make realistic datasets feasible where resource requirements previously prevented experimentation. They also release benchmarks spanning diverse realistic scenarios, providing a way to evaluate an algorithm’s overall performance. The contribution therefore combines a faster research tool with shared evaluation settings for using it.
neurips-2024-texttt-pfl-research-simulat.tldr: pfl-research accelerates private federated learning simulations, reporting 7–72× speedups on common cross-device setups.

paragraphs: WaveAttack studies backdoor attacks that manipulate training samples or training processes to mislead a neural network. The paper identifies two weaknesses in earlier approaches: poisoned images can look noticeably altered, and their internal representations can shift enough to aid detection. Its objective is to improve attack effectiveness while preserving the visual fidelity of manipulated images.

The method uses the Discrete Wavelet Transform to obtain high-frequency image features for constructing subtle triggers. It also introduces asymmetric frequency obfuscation, with an adaptive residual used during training and inference to strengthen the triggers’ impact. These components connect the frequency-based representation with the attack’s behavior across the two stages.

The authors report greater effectiveness than state-of-the-art backdoor methods, along with improved image fidelity. Reported improvements reach 28.27% for PSNR and 1.61% for SSIM, with a reduction of up to 70.59% in IS. The findings show that, in the evaluated comparisons, a more effective attack can also leave images closer to their originals. This makes visual fidelity an important part of the paper’s assessment of backdoor stealth.
neurips-2024-waveattack-asymmetric-frequ.tldr: WaveAttack uses frequency-based triggers and adaptive residuals to improve backdoor effectiveness while preserving image fidelity.

paragraphs: A model can predict dynamical data with low test error yet fail to reproduce the system’s physical behavior. The paper highlights statistical moments and Lyapunov exponents as examples of properties that ordinary prediction accuracy can miss. It develops an alternative view of generalization for learned dynamics that explicitly addresses these longer-term statistical characteristics.

The proposed framework uses ergodic theory to define and analyze whether neural representations emulate underlying invariant physical measures. It covers classes of ergodic systems, including chaotic ones. This shifts attention toward the statistical behavior generated by the learned system, providing a way to assess physical fidelity beyond conventional test error.

The theoretical results explain failures of regression-based learning of dynamical generators, including Neural ODEs, and why incorporating Jacobian information during training improves statistical accuracy. The authors verify their results on several ergodic chaotic systems with MLPs, ResNets, Fourier Neural layers, and recurrent networks. The contribution connects a more physically meaningful notion of generalization with a specific training ingredient that helps learned dynamics reproduce the statistics examined in the work.
neurips-2024-when-are-dynamical-systems-.tldr: An ergodic-theory framework explains why low prediction error can miss physical statistics and why Jacobian information improves learned dynamics.

paragraphs: XLand-MiniGrid provides grid-world environments and tools for studying agents that learn to adapt across tasks. Its design combines the diversity and depth associated with XLand with the simplicity of MiniGrid. The aim is to make large-scale meta-reinforcement learning experimentation accessible while retaining tasks that meaningfully challenge adaptive agents.

The suite is implemented in JAX and designed for high scalability, with potential execution on GPU or TPU accelerators. It includes pre-sampled benchmarks containing millions of distinct tasks at varying difficulty levels. Ready-to-use baselines give researchers a starting point for training, connecting the task collection with an immediately usable experimental workflow.

A preliminary analysis examines scaling and generalization. The baseline implementations reach millions of training steps per second, and the evaluation confirms that the proposed benchmarks are challenging. These findings establish both computational throughput and task difficulty as features of the suite. The contribution is an open-source foundation for experiments that require many varied tasks, with early evidence that substantial scale can be achieved through its implementation.
neurips-2024-xland-minigrid-scalable-met.tldr: XLand-MiniGrid offers scalable grid-world benchmarks with millions of tasks and fast baselines for studying adaptive reinforcement-learning agents.
